title: Τοῖχος καὶ πάλος
part: The Wall and the Stake (Chambry 337 · Perry 270)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 337 (= Perry 270). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Τοῖχος σπαραττόμενος ὑπὸ πάλου βιαίως ἐφώνει· « Τί με σπαράττεις μηδὲν ἠδικηκότα ; »
sentences.tr: Toichos sparattomenos hypo palou biaiōs ephōnei· « Ti me sparatteis mēden ēdikēkota ; »
sentences.l: A wall, being violently torn apart by a stake, was crying out: « Why do you tear me apart, when I have done you no wrong? »
sentences.n: The word Chambry prints is πάλος, which the lexica give as the lot cast in a drawing; the sense the fable needs is the stake or peg being driven into the wall, and how the word came by it is not certain — the Latin palus, 'stake', is the obvious neighbour. The reading is Chambry's and is left as printed. μηδέν rather than οὐδέν with the participle gives ἠδικηκότα a conditional-causal colour, 'seeing that I have done no wrong'; the perfect looks at the wrong as a standing fact.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὅς· « Οὐκ ἐγώ, φησίν, αἴτιος τούτου, ἀλλ’ ὁ ὄπισθεν σφοδρῶς με τύπτων. »
sentences.tr: Kai hos· « Ouk egō, phēsin, aitios toutou, all’ ho opisthen sphodrōs me typtōn. »
sentences.l: And it: « It is not I, » it says, « that am to blame for this, but the one behind who strikes me hard. »
sentences.n: καὶ ὅς is the old idiom in which the relative does duty for a demonstrative, 'and he' — here the stake, answering the wall; it is standard in the give and take of these dialogues. φησίν is a present in a past narrative, the historic present, and the English keeps it. The one behind is the man with the mallet: the stake is driven, and passes the blame on to the hand that drives it. Chambry prints no moral for this fable: the stake's answer is the last thing on the page before the next fable's number. Ten fables in the collection end this way.
